newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin cuts short holiday, Kremlin blames weather.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin cuts short holiday, Kremlin blames weather.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin unexpectedly broke off his holiday and returned to Moscow on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, blaming bad weather at the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
The Kremlin denied the 66-year-old leader, who had heart bypass surgery last November and pneumonia in January, was ill.

A spokesman said he was met at the airport by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who briefed him on the recent flare-up in violence around the secessionist region of Chechnya and other issues. Yeltsin had been in Sochi for 12 days apart from a short trip to Moscow last week to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

The Kremlin leader, then still in Sochi, was shown on television discussing Chechnya with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov. He was also shown going over the latest economic reform measures with First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.
Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky ruled out any health reason for Yeltsin's return to Moscow from the resort.
"His departure is linked to just one circumstance -- bad weather," Yastrzhembsky told a Russian reporter who asked if the move could be linked to illness.

Television pictures showed sunny weather in Sochi, which is in the region where two bomb attacks have killed at least four people over the past two weeks. Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had decided to return on Monday before the weather improved.
The situation around Chechnya, where 21 months of war between Moscow troops and rebels ended in a shaky truce in August, has deteriorated badly in the past week.
Bombs in two towns, a few hundred km (miles) from Sochi, killed at least four and injured dozens. A senior official of a region bordering Chechnya was shot dead on Wednesday.

Senior Russian and separatist officials met in the Chechen capital Grozny on Wednesday and issued a joint call to Yeltsin and Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov to meet quickly to conclude long stalled negotiations on a lasting settlement.

Kulikov said after meeting Yeltsin that police were taking steps to reinforce security in southern Russia but were not planning to send any fresh troops. "There are no plans to build up troops in the area," he told Russian Public Television.
"We have taken certain measures to prevent the infiltration of criminals from Chechnya," Kulikov said. "But this does not mean at all sealing off the border between Russia and Chechnya."
"What we want is a full control over it," he added.
Chechen separatist leaders have denied any part in the attacks which they said were "dirty tricks" by Russia.
Nemtsov briefed Yeltsin on the next steps in a government anti-corruption campaign and on plans to impose tighter state control over the alcohol market.
Nemtsov, appointed last month to a team of young reformers, faces the unenviable task of tackling powerful vested interests in the Russian economy which have starved the budget of cash.

A Kremlin spokesman in Moscow said Yeltsin would return to his Gorky-9 residence, west of the capital on Wednesday evening. He had recorded a radio address to the nation to be broadcast on Thursday, when Russians celebrate Labour Day. Opposition communists are expected to hold big May Day rallies in Moscow.
Yeltsin has had a busy schedule since returning from illness in February. However, officials said he had no plans to meet visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday.
Next week he is due to meet Spanish King Juan Carlos and on May 27 he expects to travel to Paris where he has said he wants to sign a partnership deal with NATO.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Wednesday Moscow was still aiming for a May 27 deal but again urged the alliance, which plans to invite in some of Moscow's former allies in July, not to move its military might into new member states.
